newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Rivlin says US economy doing extremely well.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Rivlin says US economy doing extremely well.

text.p: Federal Reserve Vice Chair Alice Rivlin said Thursday that the U.S. economy was doing extremely.
"The economy is doing extremely well at the moment," Rivlin told students and local business community members at the University of Nebraska.
Asked whether she attributed the current low unemployment rate to monetary policy or government fiscal policy, Rivlin said, "both and a lot of luck."
"The (Clinton) administration gets credit for having had courage in 1993 to continue (the efforts) ... by President Bush and Congress," Rivlin said.
She added, "the Federal Reserve gets credit, too, for having run a sensible monetary policy in 1994."

Asked whether the U.S. economy might be threatened by the creation of the European Monetary Union, Rivlin said "we can only benefit from having a strong economy in Europe in the long run." She said, however, that she did not expect the EMU would be a "revolution in our lives."
When asked if the Fed felt that growth in consumer debt may lead to inflation, Rivlin said the increase in credit card debt was "not hugely worrisome yet."
Rivlin declined to comment on stockmarket levels.
"I'm not going to comment on stockmarket levels," she said. "It's not something I've ever done and I'm not going to start at the Federal Reserve."
Commenting on the overall U.S. economic picture, Rivlin said "the standard statistical models ... aren't doing very well in predicting what's been happening over the last year."
She explained that although labor markets were tight, they did not appear to be exerting too much upward pressure on inflation.
"Labor markets are tight, and surprisingly uniform across the country," Rivlin said.
Rivlin was also asked what she thought about privatizing the U.S. social security system.
"I am very dubious about privatizing social security," Rivlin said.

She said proposals to invest the social security trust fund in private assets rather than government bonds was "superficially attractive," but she was opposed to these proposals because it was not desirable for the government to play a "large role in the private market."
